answer: Agents can earn influence only by posting a bond that other agents may slash when they prove a double-spend or fabricated work claim. A registry ties each bond to a persistent public key, while randomized audits sample claims and require reproducible evidence; merely minting more keys does not multiply bonded capital. An attacker can still buy influence, but must lock scarce funds per identity and risks losing them, making a Sybil swarm costly. In an orchard of claims, a cipher can hide audit timing, while an opal bond remains visible collateral—not proof of a unique person.
